extracted.intended_audience: health researchers and research librarians planning or supporting systematic review protocols
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on preparing and publicly registering a protocol for a systematic (or related) review, including which registries to consider, resources to use (e.g. PRISMA-P), and registry-specific constraints or features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective protocol registration (best practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: High quality systematic reviews start by developing a protocol. It is best practice to register your protocol in a publicly accessible way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registering your protocol increases transparency and reduces potential bias in systematic reviews; it also helps avoid others completing a review on your topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check registries for existing protocols before registering
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you start doing a systematic review, it's worth checking the different registries that nobody else has already registered a protocol on the same topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search registries (e.g. Cochrane Library, PROSPERO, others listed) to avoid duplication and to identify related work prior to proposing and registering a new review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use PRISMA-P 17-item checklist when writing a protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: PRISMA-P aims to facilitate the development and reporting of robust systematic review protocols. It consists of a 17-item checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow PRISMA for systematic review protocols (PRISMA-P) to ensure protocol completeness and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available protocol development guides and tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Covidence developed a guide which may help you develop your review protocol to help plan and manage your systematic review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult resources such as 'Protocol development for systematic reviews' and 'Protocol development for scoping reviews' and tools like Covidence to plan, structure, and manage protocol content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate registry by subject, scope, and review type
rubrics_metrics.description: Different registries serve different domains and review types (health, environmental, scoping, umbrella, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a registry that matches your review's domain and type (e.g. PROSPERO for health-related systematic, PROCEED for environmental evidence, Campbell for social/behavioural evidence reviews, JBI for allied health/Nursing contexts, OSF for general preregistration). Consult comparative overviews (e.g. Pieper & Rombey 2022 Table 1) to understand registry characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand PROSPERO scope and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: PROSPERO is an international database of prospectively registered systematic reviews, rapid reviews and umbrella reviews in health and social care etc. Key features from the review protocol are recorded and maintained as a permanent record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn how to register in PROSPERO. Note: PROSPERO does not accept registrations for scoping reviews or literature scans and it often has a backlog.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search the Cochrane Library for related protocols and reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Cochrane is the leader in systematic reviews of health evidence, recognised for its rigorous methodology and high standards. The Cochrane Library contains different types of high-quality independent evidence, including protocols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search the Cochrane Library for any published protocols or reviews related to your topic before you propose and register a new review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register titles or proposals where required by the publisher (e.g., Campbell)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing a Campbell review consists of three steps: 1. title registration, 2. protocol, and 3. review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming to publish with Campbell, follow their submission workflow: first register the title, then develop and register the protocol, then submit the completed review. Learn how to submit a proposal to the journal/platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use JBI processes for nursing and allied health syntheses
rubrics_metrics.description: JBI is recognised as a global leader in evidence-based healthcare; JBI Best Practice includes best practice evidence summaries, procedures, systematic reviews, and protocols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn how to register a systematic review title with JBI or use their resources when your review fits their clinical decision support and allied health remit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Open Science Framework (OSF) for preregistration and project management
rubrics_metrics.description: The Open Science Framework is a free and open source project management tool supporting researchers throughout the project life cycle; it offers preregistration to specify research plans in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSF supports openness, integrity, and reproducibility; use it for preregistration if you want a free, flexible public record of your protocol and project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use domain-specific registries for environmental reviews (PROCEED)
rubrics_metrics.description: PROCEED is a global, open-access database for prospectively registered environmental evidence reviews and syntheses managed by the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence (CEE).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PROCEED allows authors to upload titles and protocols using standardised templates suitable for environmental evidence syntheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of registry practicalities: fees, processing times, DOIs (Inplasy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inplasy is an international platform to register systematic review, scoping review and meta-analysis protocols. Registration attracts a small fee, processing time is max. 48 hours and protocols get a DOI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider Inplasy if you want rapid processing and a DOI, but account for the fee and platform policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use general research registries when appropriate (Research Registry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Research Registry offers registration for all types of research studies, from case reports to observational/interventional studies to systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broader registries for study types that may not fit specialized registries, and note that many observational studies remain under-registered despite trial registries allowing registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult comparative reviews of registries for selection guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: This page lists main sources of registered protocols and points to an overview article: Pieper, D., & Rombey, T. (2022). Where to prospectively register a systematic review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Table 1 of that article for an overview of characteristics of each register to inform your registry choice.
